episode_title: How tech workers actually feel about AI in 2026 | Annual AI sentiment survey (Noam Segal)

summary.overview: AI is having an unusually large and divisive effect on tech workers’ professional identities. In the second annual tech sentiment survey of roughly 6,000 people across product, engineering, design, research, marketing, and other roles, about half feel amplified and energized, while the rest feel uncertain, destabilized, or diminished. At the same time, burnout is rising, optimism is falling, and many workers enjoy their current jobs while feeling pessimistic about where their careers are headed.

takeaways.detail: The survey follows last year’s “Burned Out but Optimistic” findings and is intended to become an annual measure of tech sentiment. The researchers say it is unusually broad in scope, covering feelings about AI, layoffs, burnout, careers, and work across roles, levels, and company sizes.

AI’s effect on professional identity is the strongest factor the survey found—roughly three times larger than effects previously associated with one’s manager or being a founder. Only 3% said AI had not shifted their professional identity: 50% feel amplified, 27% feel their role is being redefined, 14% feel destabilized, and 5% feel diminished.

The researchers grouped workers into four emotional archetypes: energized workers (41%), who feel AI has made building fun again; a conflicted or ambivalent middle (35%), who are enjoying the work but feel uncertain about the future; disoriented workers, whose roles keep shifting; and resentful workers (12%), who feel pressured to use AI and are unhappy with the result.

These AI-identity groups correlate strongly with other measures. Moving from amplified to diminished corresponds to lower career optimism, higher burnout and layoff anxiety, and less willingness to recommend one’s role to someone entering tech.

Burnout has worsened substantially: the share reporting more than moderate burnout rose from 44.7% in 2025 to 54.7% in 2026. Optimism about the future of one’s role and career fell from 54.8% to 48.7%. The speakers connect this to AI increasing output expectations rather than reducing workloads.

Despite the burnout, many people still enjoy their work. AI lets people explore interests outside their formal roles and build things that previously seemed technically impossible. The tension is that the same technology is exciting, demanding, and difficult to switch off.

Layoff anxiety is widespread: 72% are worried to some extent about being laid off, and 41.2% are at least moderately worried. However, “losing my job to AI” ranked second-to-last among concerns; the leading fear was being expected to do more for the same pay, followed by an unsustainable pace of work and technological change.

Nearly everyone—97.2%—said AI makes them better at their job to some degree, and almost half said it makes them “very much” or “extremely” better. But respondents often meant they could produce more, faster, not that the work was higher quality. They also described declining judgment, skill atrophy, and “cognitive rot” when they accept AI output without applying their own thinking.

Curiosity and excitement were the two most common emotions, alongside overwhelm, conflict, tiredness, anxiety, and hope. Noam described this as “smiling exhaustion”: people feel newly capable and energized, but there is no off switch and the rules keep changing.

Designers and researchers reported the most negative sentiment across several measures, including feeling destabilized or diminished, anxiety about AI replacing them, and willingness to recommend their roles. Noam stressed that this reflects how they currently feel, not a conclusion that design or research is disappearing; he argued that taste, judgment, quality, and thoughtful product development remain important.

No one had a positive NPS-like score for recommending their tech role to someone entering the industry—not even founders. More senior workers were more likely to recommend their roles than individual contributors, while designers and researchers were least likely. People generally reported enjoying their current roles, but were more pessimistic about what those roles might look like in one to five years.

Founders and people at smaller companies were the most optimistic, least burned out, least worried about layoffs, and most excited about AI. Burnout rose consistently with company size, although even founders had significant burnout and generally would not recommend founding a company to others.

Managers were a major determinant of well-being. Only about 25% rated their manager highly effective, while 36% rated them ineffective; more effective managers were associated with substantially higher job enjoyment and lower burnout. The speakers suggest companies invest more in managers and that employees pay close attention to who they would report to.

For employees, the survey’s recommendations were to go deep on a few meaningful AI-enabled tasks rather than become an overextended generalist, monitor workload and renegotiate scope with managers, invest in the manager relationship, consider smaller companies or founding a company, and seek strong mentorship—especially early in one’s career. For leaders, the recommendations were to invest in managers, prevent AI-driven expectations from becoming unsustainable, protect entry-level development, and support functions feeling particularly destabilized.

The conversation also touched on AI guilt, especially among early-career workers who feel using AI is “cheating.” Noam encouraged people to learn to use the technology rather than feel guilty about it, while still maintaining deliberate thinking and judgment.

quotes.text: We’re in the second inning of a massive shift. No one knows how it will end, but all you can do is keep taking at-bats.
The speed AI unlocked got plowed straight back into expectations.
The productivity gains are real, but the quality of the work and the sharpness of the person producing it are taking a hit.
